title: Applied Neuroscience: Rewiring the Fear-Driven Mind with Brain/Computer Interface Technology
coreMove: Neurofeedback is a training route, not a miracle: use real-time signals to reward steadier rhythms, then keep claims tied to skilled practice and research.

exampleSpecs.stakes: Ernest Hartmann's Boston State Hospital sleep laboratory shows why EEG tracings can reveal regulation problems ordinary symptom reports miss.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Use the sleep-lab trace as a doorway into regulation rather than as a diagnostic shortcut.

exampleSpecs.stakes: Sebern Fisher's 2007 neurofeedback work with Lisa shows how severe dissociation may need a regulation route beyond verbal insight.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Frame neurofeedback as active training for dysregulation rather than passive monitoring.

exampleSpecs.stakes: Alexander McFarlane's 2000 work makes irrelevant information a clinical problem rather than a classroom nuisance.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Show poor filtering during an ordinary task, outside direct traumatic reminders.

exampleSpecs.audience: clinicians translating EEG insight into practice
exampleSpecs.stakes: EEG tracings from the Hartmann sleep-lab tradition matter only when a session tracks whether regulation changes the person's lived state.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Connect visible brain rhythms to present-moment regulation without making the equipment the hero.

exampleSpecs.stakes: The promise of neurofeedback needs research caution, especially when EEG frequency-band language can be oversold.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Temper enthusiasm about delta, theta, alpha, and beta with disciplined evidence claims.

exampleSpecs.audience: program leaders deciding how to evaluate a new service
exampleSpecs.stakes: Lisa's severe childhood abuse and neurofeedback improvement can motivate a program without being treated as proof of universal efficacy.
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Turn a dramatic case into a disciplined evidence plan.
